blocks.p: Any reasonably well-behaved periodic function can be rebuilt out of sines and cosines. For a function $f(x)$ with period $2\pi$:
where the coefficients are found by integrating over one full period:

blocks.math: a_0 = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\,dx, \qquad a_n = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos nx\,dx, \qquad b_n = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\sin nx\,dx

blocks.p: For a general period $2L$ on $(-L, L)$, replace $nx$ by $\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}$ everywhere and $\dfrac{1}{\pi}$ by $\dfrac{1}{L}$ in front of each integral.

sections.heading: Shortcuts for odd and even functions

blocks.p: If $f(x)$ is **odd** (symmetric about the origin), every $a_n$ (including $a_0$) is automatically zero, since cosine is even and an odd-times-even integrand over a symmetric interval vanishes. Only the sine terms survive.

If $f(x)$ is **even** (symmetric about the $y$-axis), it's the other way round: every $b_n = 0$, and only $a_0$ and the cosine terms survive. In both cases the remaining integrals can be taken over $(0, \pi)$ and doubled.

sections.heading: Worked example: the Fourier series of f(x) = x

blocks.p: Find the Fourier series of $f(x) = x$ on $(-\pi, \pi)$.
**Solution:** $f(x)=x$ is odd, so $a_0 = 0$ and every $a_n = 0$. Only $b_n$ needs computing, and since $x\sin nx$ is even, the integral over $(-\pi,\pi)$ is twice the integral over $(0,\pi)$:

blocks.math: \int_0^\pi x\sin nx\,dx = \left[-\dfrac{x\cos nx}{n}\right]_0^\pi + \dfrac{1}{n}\int_0^\pi \cos nx\,dx = -\dfrac{\pi\cos n\pi}{n} + \dfrac{1}{n}\left[\dfrac{\sin nx}{n}\right]_0^\pi

blocks.p: The second term vanishes since $\sin n\pi = 0$ for every integer $n$, and $\cos n\pi = (-1)^n$:

sections.heading: What the series does at a jump

blocks.p: Under the usual (Dirichlet) conditions, the series equals $f(x)$ wherever $f$ is continuous. At a jump it converges to the **average** of the values on either side.

The series for $x$ shows this. Repeated with period $2\pi$, the function jumps from $\pi$ down to $-\pi$ at $x = \pi$. Every term $\sin n\pi$ is 0 there, so the series gives $0 = \dfrac{\pi + (-\pi)}{2}$, the midpoint of the jump.

list: **Mixing the two conventions for the constant.** With $a_0 = \dfrac{1}{\pi}\displaystyle\int f\,dx$, the series starts with $\dfrac{a_0}{2}$. Some books define $a_0$ with $\dfrac{1}{2\pi}$ and start with $a_0$. Use one convention throughout.
**Computing coefficients you already know are zero.** Check odd or even first: it removes half the work.
**Forgetting $\cos n\pi = (-1)^n$ and $\sin n\pi = 0$.** Almost every boundary term simplifies through these two facts.
**Keeping $nx$ for a period other than $2\pi$.** On $(-L, L)$ the arguments become $\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}$.
**Claiming the series equals $f$ at a discontinuity.** It gives the average of the two one-sided values there.

exam.note: Fourier series are part of the Engineering Mathematics section in GATE EC, EE and IN (and several other papers), and GATE EC also builds on them in Signals and Systems. They are a standard unit of first-year engineering mathematics, usually alongside Laplace transforms.

related.intro: Fourier series and Laplace transforms are the two core tools engineering math uses to turn a hard problem in the time domain into an easier one somewhere else.
